newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian zinc output seen up 4.3 pct - ABARE.
newsitem.headline: Australian zinc output seen up 4.3 pct - ABARE.

text.p: Australian zinc mine production is forecast to rise 4.3 percent to 1.10 million tonnes in 1997/98 (July/June), the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said on Tuesday.
In its June quarter report, ABARE said mine production was estimated to have risen by 1.9 percent in 1996/97.

Increases at the Northern Territory McArthur River and Woodcutters mines and Pasminco Ltd's Broken Hill mine were partially offset by lower production at MIM Holding Ltd's Hilton mine and the Woodlawn mine in New South Wales.
MIM operates McArthur River, Normandy Mining Ltd owns Woodcutters and Denehurst Ltd owns Woodlawn.

ABARE said the forecast 1997/98 production rise was due to the McArthur River mine reaching full capacity and co-product zinc production starting at the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd's new Cannington lead-silver-zinc mine in Queensland.
Australian zinc export earnings are estimated to have risen by 4.3 percent in 1996/97 due to increased concentrate exports and an almost 10 percent rise in the average world zinc price.
Production rises were expected to lead to further increases in exports of concentrates and an increase in refined metal exports in 1997/98, ABARE said.
"These rises, together with increased prices, are forecast to result in Australian export earnings from zinc increasing strongly to A$1.1 billion," the bureau said.
Average world prices for zinc are forecast to rise by 25 percent in calendar 1997, and a further 11 percent in 1998 due to falling stocks and rising consumption.
"Reports suggest that the recent price increases have also been supported by investment fund buying in anticpation of further tightening in the market," ABARE said.

The level of Chinese activity remains a key uncertainty, it said. In 1996, Chinese zinc exports to Western countries slowed the rate of the stocks fall, and the current decline in stocks could be moderated if China were to resume exports on a similar scale to 1996, the bureau said.

However, ABARE said that despite Chinese exports data for January to April 1997 showing a substantial year on year rise, western world stocks were forecast to ease to just over five weeks of consumption at the end of 1998.

Apparent world consumption of zinc was forecast to rise by 3.5 percent in 1997, reflecting expected stronger industrial production growth in OECD countries and continued strong economic and industrial production growth in Asia.

In 1998, consumption is forecast to increase by 2.2 percent, a forecast which assumes slower industrial production growth in the U.S. and Japan and slower, although still strong, growth in Asia, particulalry China, ABARE said.

World mine production of zinc is expected to be steady in 1997, then rise by 4.7 percent in 1998 to 7.55 million tonnes. ABARE said the 1997 forecast reflected offsetting increase and decreases from several mines, with the loss of output due to the closure of Canada's Faro mine balanced by increases at new and reactivated mines in Spain, Peru and Ireland and a lift in other mines output, including McArthur River.
The 1998 forecast lift reflects the expected recommencement of operations at Faro later this year and two new Australian mines, Cannington and Blendvale in Western Australia.
